title: A bet on staying put
objectives: Build a butterfly from three strikes.
Read its tent-shaped payoff, cost, maximum profit and break-evens.

screens.prose: Three calls on a share at £100.00, all with the same expiry. You buy one struck at £95.00, sell **two** struck at £100.00 and buy one struck at £105.00. The bold line is the whole position.
screens.question: The share ends at £102.00. What does the position pay?

hints.text: Work out each strike at £102.00, then add with signs.
Each of the two sold calls is exercised against you for £2.00.
+7 from the £95.00 call, −2 × 2 from the sold calls, 0 from the £105.00 call.

feedback.correct: +£7.00, then −£4.00 on the two sold calls.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count each leg at £102.00, with the sold ones against you.

byKey.first: You counted only the £95.00 call. The two sold calls are exercised against you.
byKey.added: You added the sold calls' payoffs. Those belong to their buyers, so they come off.
byKey.single: You took off £2.00 once. You sold two calls at £100.00, so you owe it twice.

explain.text: The £95.00 call pays $102 - 95 = 7$. Each sold call costs $102 - 100 = 2$, and there are two. The £105.00 call pays nothing, so the total is £3.00.

screens.prose: Slide the price at expiry across the range and watch the bold line. Read its label as you go.
screens.question: Which describes the payoff?

options.text: A tent: £0.00 outside £95.00 to £105.00, peaking at £5.00 at £100.00
A V: £0.00 at £100.00 and rising either side
options.why: That is the straddle's shape. Here the sold calls pull the line back down above £100.00.

options.text: A ramp: rising from £95.00 and capped at £5.00
options.why: Slide past £100.00. The two sold calls make the line fall again, back to £0.00 at £105.00.

hints.text: Look at what happens just above £100.00.

feedback.correct: It pays only near £100.00, most at £100.00 itself.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Slide above £100.00 and watch which way the line goes.

explain.text: From £95.00 the bought call climbs £1.00 a pound. Above £100.00 two sold calls take away £2.00 a pound, so the line falls. Above £105.00 the last call restores the balance, and the line stays at £0.00.

screens.prose: This tent is a **long call butterfly**: the outer strikes are the wings, the middle one the body. The £95.00 call costs £7.50, each £100.00 call £4.00, and the £105.00 call £1.50.
screens.question: What does the butterfly cost you today?

hints.text: Which calls do you buy, and which do you sell?
You sell two £100.00 calls, so you receive £4.00 twice.

feedback.correct: £9.00 paid on the wings, £8.00 received on the body.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Pay for the wings, receive for the body, and remember there are two body calls.

byKey.added: You added every premium. The two body calls are sold, so their £8.00 comes in.
byKey.single: You received £4.00 once. You sold two calls at £100.00, so £8.00 comes in.
byKey.sign: You have the sign the wrong way round. You pay £9.00 and receive £8.00, so it costs you £1.00.

explain.text: The wings cost $7.50 + 1.50 = 9.00$ and the body brings in $2 \times 4.00 = 8.00$. So the butterfly costs £1.00. It is cheap because it pays only if the share lands near £100.00.

screens.prose: Fill in the table by leg. The body column is both sold calls together, so it counts twice.
screens.question: Complete the payoff table for the butterfly.

hints.text: Do each leg on its own, then add across the row.
Above £100.00 each sold call costs $S_T - 100$, and there are two.

feedback.correct: The tent is £2.00 high at £97.00 and £103.00, and back to £0.00 at £110.00.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find each leg, with the body doubled, then add.

byKey.r2c2: Each sold call costs $103 - 100 = 3$, and you sold two.
byKey.r3c2: Each sold call costs $110 - 100 = 10$, and you sold two.

explain.text: The doubled body cancels the lower wing's rise above £100.00 and then some. The upper wing switches on at £105.00 to stop the fall. Beyond the wings the three legs sum to £0.00.

screens.prose: Here the wings are in the wrong places. The body, two sold calls, stays at £100.00. The diamonds on the price axis are the strikes of the two wings.
screens.question: Drag the two wings to make the £95.00/£100.00/£105.00 tent: £5.00 at £100.00 and £0.00 outside.

hints.text: The peak height equals the distance from the lower wing to the body.
The wings sit the same distance either side of the body.
Put the lower wing at £95.00 and the upper wing at £105.00.

feedback.correct: Wings £5.00 either side of the body.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the peak height, then check the line returns to £0.00 on the right.

byKey.on-body: A wing on top of the body cancels it. Keep each wing £5.00 away.
byKey.c1: The lower wing sets the peak: it must be £5.00 below the body for a £5.00 peak.
byKey.c3: The upper wing must sit as far above the body as the lower wing sits below. Otherwise the line misses £0.00.

explain.text: The peak is the gap from the lower wing to the body, £5.00. The line falls £1.00 a pound above the body. It reaches £0.00 exactly at the upper wing, so the wings must be equally spaced.

screens.prose: Back to the £1.00 butterfly. A colleague expects a huge move and wants the butterfly for it. Another builds it with only **one** sold call at £100.00. The share jumps to £130.00.
screens.question: What is the real butterfly's profit at £130.00?

options.why: You sold only one call at £100.00. With one body call the position keeps rising above £105.00.
£4.00 is the best case, at £100.00. Far from the body the tent pays nothing.
You counted the £95.00 call alone. The sold calls and the upper wing cancel its rise.

hints.text: What does the tent pay outside £95.00 to £105.00?
At £130.00: 35 from the lower wing, −60 from the body, 25 from the upper wing.
Payoff 0, less the £1.00 cost.

feedback.correct: A big move pays nothing, so you lose the £1.00 cost.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work out the payoff at £130.00 with both body calls, then take off £1.00.

byKey.b: With one sold call the position is a call plus a spread, not a butterfly. The body must be doubled.
byKey.c: You expected the butterfly to profit from the move. It profits only if the share stays near £100.00.

explain.text: At £130.00 the legs give $35 - 60 + 25 = 0$. You lose the £1.00 you paid. A butterfly is a bet that the share stays put, so a big move is its worst case.

screens.prose: Read the profit line of the £1.00 butterfly. The break-even markers are hidden.
screens.question: Fill in the butterfly's key numbers.

hints.text: The peak payoff is £5.00, at the body.
The tent rises from £95.00 and falls to £105.00, £1.00 a pound.
Maximum profit 5 − 1 = 4. Break-evens 95 + 1 = 96 and 105 − 1 = 104.

feedback.correct: £4.00 at best, £1.00 at worst, break-evens £96.00 and £104.00.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take the £1.00 cost off the tent, then find where it crosses zero.

byKey.r0c1: The peak payoff is £5.00. Take off the £1.00 you paid.
byKey.r1c1: Outside the wings the payoff is 0, so you lose only what you paid.
byKey.r2c1: Go up from the lower wing by the £1.00 cost.
byKey.r3c1: Come down from the upper wing by the £1.00 cost.

explain.text: The tent peaks at £5.00, so the profit peaks at £4.00. It crosses zero £1.00 inside each wing: at £96.00 and £104.00. Outside them the loss is capped at the £1.00 paid.

screens.prose: Build the same shape with puts on the same share: buy the £95.00 put for £2.50, sell two £100.00 puts for £4.00 each, buy the £105.00 put for £6.50.
screens.question: What does the put butterfly cost?

hints.text: Pay for the wings, receive for the body.
There are two body puts.

feedback.correct: £9.00 on the wings less £8.00 on the body: £1.00, as with calls.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the two sold puts as income.

byKey.added: You added every premium. The two body puts are sold, so their £8.00 comes in.
byKey.single: You received £4.00 once. You sold two puts at £100.00.
byKey.sign: You pay £9.00 and receive £8.00, so it costs you £1.00.

explain.text: The put butterfly has the same tent and the same £1.00 price as the call one. Two positions with equal payoffs must cost the same. Level 3 turns that idea into **put-call parity**.

screens.prose: Squeeze the wings in: buy the £99.00 call, sell two £100.00 calls and buy the £101.00 call.
screens.question: What is the most this butterfly can pay?

widget.label: Maximum payoff
widget.accept: £1.00: the gap from a wing to the body

hints.text: The peak equals the gap from the lower wing to the body.
The wings are £1.00 from the body.

feedback.correct: The peak is the wing gap, £1.00.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the gap between a wing and the body.

byKey.old: That was the wider butterfly. Here the wings are only £1.00 away.
byKey.width: £2.00 is the full base, from wing to wing. The peak is half of it.
byKey.zero: At £100.00 the £99.00 call pays £1.00 and the sold calls pay nothing.

explain.text: Narrow wings give a tall, thin spike on a small base. Buy many such butterflies and scale them up, and the spike pays only at £100.00. That limit is a **digital** payoff, which pays a fixed amount or nothing.

screens.prose: With equally spaced strikes $K - h$, $K$ and $K + h$, the butterfly's payoff is $$\max(S_T - K + h, 0) - 2\max(S_T - K, 0) + \max(S_T - K - h, 0).$$ It is a tent of height $h$ at $K$ and zero outside the wings. Its net premium must lie between 0 and $h$.
screens.question: Why must a butterfly's net premium be more than £0.00?

options.text: Its payoff is never negative and sometimes positive
The body is sold, so the seller always pays
options.why: You receive premium on the body, but the wings cost more. A payoff that can only help you cannot be free.
That is only for this butterfly. Any width keeps a payoff that is never below 0.

options.text: Options always cost money, whatever the legs
options.why: Spreads can earn you a net credit. The reason is the shape of this payoff.

feedback.correct: A payoff that can only help you must cost something.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look at the lowest point of the tent.

explain.text: The tent never dips below £0.00 and rises to $h$. If it were free, you would take it for nothing and sometimes collect. So the net premium lies between 0 and $h$.

screens.prose: A market maker thinks options on a £100.00 share overprice a big move. She buys the £95.00/£100.00/£105.00 butterfly for £1.00. Picture a crude market view: the share lands at £100.00 with chance $q$, or far outside the wings.
screens.question: What chance $q$ makes £1.00 a fair price for the £5.00 tent?

hints.text: The tent pays £5.00 with chance $q$ and £0.00 otherwise.
A fair price is the expected payoff, $5q$.
Solve $5q = 1$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Set the expected payoff equal to the £1.00 price.

byKey.profit: You used the £4.00 maximum profit over £5.00. Use the price over the payoff.
byKey.byprofit: You divided the price by the £4.00 maximum profit. The fair price is the expected payoff, £5.00 times $q$.
byKey.pct: Give the chance as a decimal: 20% is 0.2.

explain.text: The market's £1.00 says a 20% chance of landing near £100.00. If she thinks it is 35%, she values the tent at £1.75 and buys. Butterfly prices map out the market's chances by price. Pricing with Trees builds that map into a **risk-neutral density**.

ideas: A long butterfly buys a call at each wing and sells two at the body.
Its payoff is a tent: height $h$ at the body, zero outside the wings. It profits only if the share stays near the body.
Its net premium lies between 0 and $h$. Puts at the same strikes give the same tent at the same price.

formula.name: Butterfly payoff
formula.note: Here $x^+ = \max(x, 0)$. The body is sold twice.

summary.trap: Selling only one body call, or expecting a butterfly to gain from a large move. A big move pays nothing.

quiz.prose: The £95.00/£100.00/£105.00 call butterfly. The share ends at £98.00.
quiz.question: What does the butterfly pay?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Below the body only the £95.00 call is in the money.

byKey.peak: That is the peak, at £100.00. At £98.00 the tent is lower.
byKey.cost: You took off the £1.00 cost. The question asks for the payoff.

explain.text: At £98.00 only the £95.00 call pays: $98 - 95 = 3$. The sold calls and the upper wing pay nothing.

quiz.prose: Calls on a share at £97.00 are quoted at £8.00 (strike £90.00), £4.50 (strike £100.00) and £2.00 (strike £110.00).
quiz.question: What does the £90.00/£100.00/£110.00 call butterfly cost?

feedback.correct: £10.00 on the wings less £9.00 on the body.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Pay for the wings and receive for two body calls.

byKey.single: You received the body premium once. You sell two body calls.
byKey.added: You added every premium. The body is sold, so its premium comes in.
byKey.sign: You pay £10.00 and receive £9.00, so the butterfly costs £1.00.

explain.text: The wings cost $8.00 + 2.00 = 10.00$ and the body brings in $2 \times 4.50 = 9.00$. The net cost is £1.00, between 0 and the £10.00 peak.

quiz.prose: Four traders each describe their view of a share now at £100.00.
quiz.question: Which trader should buy the £95.00/£100.00/£105.00 butterfly?

options.text: One who expects the share to end close to £100.00
One who expects a large move but not its direction
options.why: That is a straddle's view. A large move leaves the butterfly at £0.00.

options.text: One who expects a steady rise to £120.00
options.why: At £120.00 the butterfly pays nothing. A call or a bull spread suits that view.

options.text: One who wants protection against a crash
options.why: Below £95.00 the butterfly pays nothing, so it protects nothing.

feedback.correct: The butterfly is a bet on staying put.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask where the tent pays.

explain.text: The tent pays only between £95.00 and £105.00, and most at £100.00. It suits a trader who expects calm near the body.

quiz.question: What is its maximum profit?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the peak from the wing gap, then take off the cost.

byKey.payoff: That is the maximum payoff. Take off the £0.08 you paid.
byKey.wide: You used the £5.00 peak of the wider butterfly. Here the wings are £1.00 away.
byKey.width: You used the £2.00 base as the peak. The peak is the gap from one wing to the body.

explain.text: The peak is the wing gap, £1.00, at £100.00. The maximum profit is $1.00 - 0.08 = 0.92$.
